lede: Parable reads the tools a company already works in, and shows where the work goes, what it costs, and what AI could take on. It had been giving clients that insight as slide decks. I was its product designer, and designed its first product: three experiences, and the design system behind them.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Product designer, the only one at Parable. A graphic designer made the company’s slide decks.

facts.label: How long
facts.note: To confirm: the end date. Constantin’s case study only places the design system work in the first quarter of 2026.

facts.label: Team
facts.value: A company of about twenty. I worked with the Director of product, who shaped what the product does, with the founders, and in code with the front-end engineer.
facts.note: To confirm: that the founders stay in this line beside the Director of product.

facts.label: How we defined success
facts.value: Screens that product managers and Parable’s own AI can put together from shared parts, without the product drifting further from itself, measured against five targets set for the work.
facts.note: To discuss with What we learned, at the end.

facts.label: What we achieved
facts.value: The foundation shipped, with the most important components built on it: colours cut from about 60 to 18, spacing values from 24 to 13, and chart colours from more than 50 to 12.

hero.alt: Ponder, Parable’s assistant, greets John, the CEO, with Acme drawn as an orb of 2,496 points, one per person. He picks a question about Finance, and the orb flies into the conversation, thinks, and becomes the answer: first a ring of Finance’s work, then columns ranking the workflows to automate first, from invoice matching at $1.68M a year.

blocks.milestone: Parable gave its clients insight as slide decks. Its own pipelines pulled in each client’s data, and people and AI put the decks together by hand. The next step was a product clients would use themselves.

stats.label: Three people, three separate jobs
stats.text: The CEO asks a question, someone in operations builds the answer, and the CTO connects the company’s tools. Each needed their own experience, and all three had to feel like one product.

stats.label: One system for every version of the product
stats.text: The design system had to serve any version of the product, an experiment or the live one, whether a person or Parable’s own AI put the screen together.

blocks.milestone: The Director of product shaped what the product does: Ponder, the assistant, and Parables, the answers people build. I built how it looks and moves, and the system underneath.

context.label: What we focused on, and why
context.value: The point cloud, made into the product
context.text: Parable’s decks used a cloud of points as a simple picture of AI. I made it move and grow, so a company’s own people became every chart and the assistant’s body.

context.label: How we worked
context.text: The design system started in Figma. One goal was for design and code to match exactly.

figure.alt: An early Parable product frame titled Sales Team Performance: a ring of the team’s work, a strip of activity, a list of people, and $1.2M in potential savings, with a fine dust of points drifting behind the cards.
figure.caption: An early Parable product frame, not a deck slide. The points are only dust behind the cards.

blocks.p: Acme, the sample company on these screens, is 2,496 points, one for each person. The same points make every chart.

figure.alt: The camera starts on a single point, one field engineer, and pulls back through their team and department until all of Acme is in view: an orb of 2,496 points, one per person.
figure.caption: The camera pulls back from one field engineer to all of Acme.

blocks.p: Ponder is drawn as the orb of Acme’s people. When it answers, the orb turns into the chart.

figure.alt: The orb of Acme’s people opens and its points fall into columns ranking Finance’s workflows to automate first, from invoice matching at $1.68M a year, then gather back into the orb.
figure.caption: The orb becomes a ranking of what Finance should automate first, then gathers back.

blocks.p: With the same points, Ponder shows what it’s reading. A state is a movement and one line of text, never a new colour.

figure.alt: Ponder works on where AI is saving time in Customer Success. As its log reads Zendesk, then Gong, the people each tool covers light up in the orb: 390 people, then 119.
figure.caption: As Ponder reads each tool, the people it covers light up.

blocks.milestone: Three people, three separate journeys, one system. John, the CEO, asks Ponder, in the film at the top of the page. Priya, in Finance, builds a Parable. Sam, the CTO, connects the tools.

blocks.sub: One small system behind every screen

blocks.p: It’s a short list of parts with rules: colours with one job each, where violet means AI and pink means look here, one type scale, and sizes set by where a part sits, after Linear. The charts are parts too, all made of the same points. Every screen on this page is built from it: 189 tokens, one file of parts, nothing written by hand.

figure.alt: Parts of Parable’s design system in six cells. Points: everyone at Acme as an orb, one point per person, with what each point colour means: ivory for the rest of the data, violet for AI, pink for look here, and a ghost for what Parable can’t see. Type: one scale, from a 36 point title in PP Editorial New down to a host name in code. Colours: the ground and the cream laid over it, ink at three strengths, Ponder’s violet drafting badge and a pink needs-attention flag. Ponder: a closed work log and an answer with a source pill. Controls: the Perception selector, buttons, a segmented control, tokens, badges, a key, a switch and a step row. And the same points again as a ranking of what Finance should automate first.
figure.caption: Parts of the system, drawn by the same code as every screen on this page.

blocks.p: A Parable is a plan of steps, written as plain sentences. Ponder drafts it from Priya’s question and says what it assumed. She corrects it in her team’s own words, dragging Finance’s own workflows onto a step, then reads the result as a page.

figure.alt: Priya types her question and Ponder offers to draft it. Ponder drafts six steps one at a time and lists what it assumed, including its rule for repetitive work, and every step runs. She switches to Finance’s own Perception and drags its Workflows onto step 3: before she lets go, twelve bands of points regroup into the eight workflows Finance names itself, and the step loses Ponder’s mark. She drags Ranking onto the table Ponder proposed for step 5, and the points stand up as columns. View opens on page 3, What to automate first, with the plan as six sentences beside it.
figure.caption: Ponder drafts the plan, Priya corrects it, and the result opens as a page.

blocks.p: Sam starts from a table of every tool Acme uses: what’s connected, what’s missing, and which are core, the tools a team does most of its work in. Then one product at a time, here Jira on Acme’s own servers, with exactly what Parable reads and what it never reads.

grid.alt: Parable’s Connectors page: a table of the 214 tools Acme uses, grouped by status, with filters for all, core, connected, not connected and needs attention. Gong needs attention because its key was replaced. Four core tools are not connected yet, FieldPro, Jira, GitHub and HubSpot, each with what Parable would read and how much more of Acme it would see. Below them, the connected tools, from Okta and Google Workspace for everyone to Zendesk, NetSuite, Workday and Salesforce. Parable sees 45% of how Acme works now, and would see 85% with the four missing core tools.
grid.caption: Every tool in one table. Four core tools are still missing.

grid.alt: Jira Data Center, on Acme’s own servers at jira.acme.internal. On the left, Atlassian’s products: Jira, which is core, with two instances, Cloud and Data Center, then Confluence and Jira Service Management, which are not. In the middle, the projects Parable reads (Installations, Permits, Crew scheduling), the archive it doesn’t, and the People team it never reads, by Acme’s rule; what it reads from each issue and what it never reads; and limits such as 12 months back, people shown as roles, and who can ask about it. On the right, the steps from way in to connected, a relay in Acme’s network, a read-only account, and 20,100 issues to read.
grid.caption: Jira on Acme’s own servers: which projects Parable reads, and what it never reads.

blocks.milestone: Success meant screens that product managers and Parable’s own AI can put together from shared parts, without the product drifting further from itself. The foundation shipped. The first experience shown on this page is concept work, not shipped screens.

blocks.todo: Result to confirm: does each person get to their one thing on the first day? Whether the three journeys were put in front of a CTO, someone in operations or a CEO, and what happened.

blocks.p: Next, I would build the automatic check, on the day Parable’s AI starts sending screens it put together itself to customers, so each screen is tested against the rules before anyone sees it.
